title: Result-gate rows that say what changed, how, and in what kind of thing
request:
The first gate under the new rules has many uncategorized rows: a feature step can only produce 'added', and a behavior-change step can't produce 'removed' or 'type changed'. What should happen?

(chosen: New intent (Recommended))

In result gate, it is difficult to know what's really changed in depth. For example it lists changed symbols but I can't even know what it is changing - a class? object? function?

(chosen: Fold into #7)
problem: The reviewer at a result gate can't tell from its rows what really changed. On #6's result gate, the first under per-kind categories, 12 of 30 rows showed as uncategorized: a feature step that also changes existing symbols, and a behavior-change step that also retypes or removes a field, have no category for those changes. The reviewer can't tell whether uncategorized means a step mixed kinds or the kind's list is too narrow, so the label stops carrying information. And even a categorized row only names the changed symbol: it doesn't say whether that is a class, an object, or a function, or what changed inside it, so the reviewer has to open the code to judge a change the gate exists to show.
acceptance: At a result gate, uncategorized appears only for a change that no category describes, not for an ordinary part of a step of that kind.

Every changed thing at a result gate says what kind of thing it is and where it lives, in its language's own terms for code (such as a class, a type alias, or a function) and as a kind of text for prose (such as a skill or a design doc), so the reviewer doesn't have to open the file to find out.
Every changed thing says what changed inside it, not only that it changed, so the reviewer can judge the change against the plan without opening the code.
The added detail doesn't bury what needs attention: unplanned, missing, breaking, and inferred rows still come first, and each row stays readable at a glance.
#6's result gate is the worked example both halves are checked against.

openQuestions.text: When a thing changes what kind it is, such as an object becoming a class, what should its row say?
openQuestions.proposal: Show both kinds, before and after (object → class), under the existing type changed category, rather than adding a new category. #6 Q1 kept one small shared list so a word means the same thing in every kind, and the before and after already tell the reviewer what happened.

openQuestions.text: For the uncategorized rows: should each kind's category list widen to the changes that ordinarily come with it, or should steps split finer so each stays within its kind's list?
openQuestions.proposal: Widen the lists, checked against #6's 12 rows: a feature step can also change existing things (renamed, type changed, value changed, behavior changed), and a behavior-change step can also produce removed and type changed. Splitting would make the planner cut one logical change into several steps just to satisfy the labels, against one step per logical change, and give the reviewer more steps for the same work. Asked last because showing what changed inside a thing (Q4) may turn some of those rows into members added, which feature already allows.

decisions.question: Should the two halves, rows that land in uncategorized and rows that don't say what kind of thing changed or what changed in it, stay one intent?
Which kinds of thing must a row be able to name, and does this cover prose rows (instructions, docs) as well as code rows?
decisions.answer: Language's own kinds: use what the language's compiler calls it (in TypeScript: type alias, accessor, namespace...). Prose rows name a kind too: what kind of text it is (skill, CLAUDE.md, design doc, hook prompt).

decisions.question: What must a reviewer be able to see for each changed thing?
decisions.answer: Kind, home, category, diff (Recommended): what kind of thing it is, where it lives (the containing class or module), its category, and the before and after of the part that changed.

decisions.question: How much of what changed inside a thing is enough, and when is it too long?
decisions.answer: One level, body behind toggle (Recommended): one level down, only what changed (a class's changed members, a function's old and new signature, a value's old and new value, a behavior's changed condition and outcome). A body diff sits behind a toggle that starts closed.
